channel.title: OSA Paper Podcast
channel.description:
Every day, one new paper on obstructive sleep apnea surgery: hypoglossal nerve stimulation, palate surgery including barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, tongue base, skeletal and nasal procedures, patient selection and comparators. Every episode summarizes the paper, walks through it as a teaching round, places it against a 440-paper evidence library, and ends with whether it should change practice.
Episodes are written and narrated by an AI system working from the full text of each paper and the host's curated library of digests, under rules set by the host. They are reviewed for teaching, not for patient care. Nothing here is medical advice.
Episode guide and subscribe links: https://www.sleepapneaimplant.org/podcast
Produced by Ryan Nord, MD (VCU Health). Disclosures: consultant to AvivoMed; previously a consultant to Inspire Medical Systems (ended 2025) and Medtronic. No company funds or reviews this podcast.

item.title: Systematic Review on the Safety of Outpatient Upper Airway Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients in Ambulatory Surgical Centers - Journal of otolaryngology
item.itunes:title: Systematic Review on the Safety of Outpatient Upper Airway Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients in Ambulatory Surgical Centers - Journal of otolaryngology
item.description:
The take-home point. In Dr. Nord's practice, airway-surgery patients like the ones in this review are kept for twenty-three-hour observation, and that includes B-R-P. The decision this paper touches is whether B-R-P patients could move to same-day discharge from a surgery center. This review does not supply the evidence for that move. Its patients were mostly classic U-triple-P patients treated in hospitals. And its headline admission rate, a little more than one in twenty, sits above the authors' own three percent bar.
What it does add is useful for counseling and for teaching. Serious respiratory events after these operations cluster in the first few hours. Most early events are desaturations, and how often you find them depends on how closely you look. In at least one cohort, a higher body mass index and A-H-I were linked to higher odds of desaturation in the recovery room.
For patients asking about weight, here is one figure that is easy to share. In the Rotenberg group's twenty thirteen cohort, a higher body mass index was linked to roughly two point seven times the odds of desaturating in the recovery room, though the paper does not say exactly which comparison that figure describes. Also, another included series found no such link. A second figure comes from the Shave surgery-center series. There, patients with a body mass index over forty-five were sent to the hospital instead.
For residents in the operating room and clinic, the lesson is about the patient's whole course. A twenty-four-hour window captures the airway story. It misses the bleeding story, which can arrive anywhere from several days to two weeks later.
On its own, this review is not the evidence that would move B-R-P patients from observation to same-day discharge. One kind of study would change that. It would be a prospective surgery-center series of modern pharyngoplasty. It would classify patients by intention and use one desaturation definition. And its thirty-day follow-up would capture readmissions at any hospital.
To restate the headline one last time. Across the four studies that reported it, unplanned admission for a medical reason averaged a little more than one in twenty. That is five point four percent, above the authors' own three percent goal.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Asghar M, Pang K, Asghar M, Rotenberg B. Systematic Review on the Safety of Outpatient Upper Airway Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients in Ambulatory Surgical Centers. *Journal of Otolaryngology - Head & Neck Surgery*. 2025;54. doi:10.1177/19160216251379325 https://doi.org/10.1177/19160216251379325

item.title: Association Between Perioperative Celecoxib, Acetaminophen, and Opioid Consumption After Palate Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.itunes:title: Association Between Perioperative Celecoxib, Acetaminophen, and Opioid Consumption After Palate Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.description:
The take-home point: this paper gives an adult, sleep-apnea-specific signal that scheduled celecoxib goes with modestly less opioid use on the first day, and it sharpens how patients are counseled.
Here is why it fits. Dr. Nord performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, and airway-surgery patients like these are kept for twenty-three-hour observation. The first-day window in this paper lines up closely with that observation stay.
The decision it affects is whether scheduled celecoxib, before and after surgery, belongs in the multimodal plan for barbed reposition pharyngoplasty. What the paper adds, in words worth remembering, is that more celecoxib went with a little less opioid. Each hundred milligrams went with about two point seven fewer morphine milligram equivalents, after adjustment.
It also adds to counseling. Almost everyone still received an opioid, two hundred and five of two hundred and ten. That supports telling patients to expect some opioid on the first day, rather than promising an opioid-free recovery. Tonsillectomy went with about thirty-one more milligram equivalents. Barbed reposition pharyngoplasty is typically done with tonsillectomy, so its patients look more like the higher-need group, though carrying that figure over to barbed work is an inference. Patients with autoimmune or immunosuppressive conditions may need more, though that group was small.
Two things the paper does not license. It does not show that acetaminophen fails, so it is no reason to drop it. And it does not show that celecoxib is safe for bleeding, with ketorolac's adult tonsillectomy signal a separate concern.
Confidence is modest. This is an association, tangled with a change in era, in a cohort with no barbed reposition pharyngoplasty patients. What would move it is a randomized trial in barbed pharyngoplasty, with pain scores, opioid use at home through two weeks, and bleeding through thirty days. A negative trial would move it the other way.
For the residents Dr. Nord teaches in the operating room and clinic, the lesson is simple. Read the units, and read the era, before you read the p value.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Badash I, Wong S, Biju K, Hur K, Commesso E, Kezirian EJ. "Association Between Perioperative Celecoxib, Acetaminophen, and Opioid Consumption After Palate Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea." *Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery* 2025;172(2):678–685. DOI: 10.1002/ohn.1069. PMID: not printed in PDF. Received July 6, 2024; accepted November 11, 2024. Presented at the AAO-HNSF 2024 Annual Meeting, September 28–October 1, 2024, Miami Beach. https://doi.org/10.1002/ohn.1069

item.title: A Randomized Trial of Nefopam for Postoperative Pain Management in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients Undergoing Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
item.itunes:title: A Randomized Trial of Nefopam for Postoperative Pain Management in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients Undergoing Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
item.description:
The take-home point. Nefopam did not lower morphine after UPPP. On the first day, patients used a median of seven milligrams with nefopam and five with placebo, both remarkably little. On top of a strong scheduled regimen, the extra drug bought nothing this trial could detect.
The decision this paper informs is whether to add nefopam to a pain regimen after palate surgery. It supports the authors' advice against routine add-on use. Nefopam is not approved in the United States. So for American surgeons, the broader lesson is about adjuncts in general. An adjunct needs room to work, and a strong backbone may leave little.
It also doesn't transfer to barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, or B-R-P. Dr. Nord performs B-R-P, not the classic resection UPPP with tonsillectomy studied here. The literature has no analgesia trial for B-R-P at all. So the five-to-seven-milligram figure shouldn't be quoted to a B-R-P patient as an expected recovery.
Where the paper adds most is counseling. In both arms, swallowing hurt more than resting, especially in the first week. Resting pain settled within that week. Mild swallowing pain lingered, and by the second week most patients had no residual pain. That's a clear, honest script for the preoperative visit, and the Delphi's day-five-to-seven peak backs it up.
On safety, no respiratory depression in fifty-one patients is reassuring, but it is far too few to relax monitoring. Airway-surgery patients like these are kept for twenty-three-hour observation in Dr. Nord's practice, and nothing in this trial argues otherwise.
For residents in the operating room and clinic, this paper is a clean case for one habit. Before you believe a negative trial, check the power calculation.
Confidence that nefopam adds little on top of a strong regimen in young, healthy patients: moderate. Confidence that this holds for older, heavier, higher-risk patients: low. What would move it? A larger multicenter trial, powered on realistic opioid use, that reports confidence intervals and tracks breathing through the first nights.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Chumpathong S, Mangmeesri P, Panyamee S, Banhiran W, Uataya M (author order partly scrambled by extraction; Uataya prints on the second author line). "A randomized trial of nefopam for postoperative pain management in obstructive sleep apnea patients undergoing uvulopalatopharyngoplasty." *European Archives of Oto-Rhino-Laryngology* 2026; volume, issue and pages not printed (online first). DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10472-w (printed). PMID: not printed in PDF. Received 8 May 2025; accepted 6 July 2026. Departments of Anesthesiology and Otorhinolaryngology, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand. Corresponding author Peerachatra Mangmeesri. item.title: Predictive Factors for Surgical Outcomes and Symptom Persistence After Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.itunes:title: Predictive Factors for Surgical Outcomes and Symptom Persistence After Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.description:
The take-home point is about selection and counseling for palate surgery. In Dr. Nord's practice that operation is BRP, and this paper is not BRP. It used no barbs, it pooled adjunct procedures in unreported numbers, and it never assessed collapse pattern with DISE. So its odds ratios do not transfer to BRP.
What it adds is a clear picture of who does well. Overall, about two in three met the success definition at three months: one hundred twenty-three of one hundred ninety-one. In Friedman stage three, it was only about one in seven: eight of fifty-nine. That sharpens the clinic conversation. A lean patient with favorable Friedman anatomy is a good palate candidate. A stage-three patient faces poor odds with palate surgery alone, and the authors themselves point toward cautious selection or multimodal treatment. Dr. Nord's practice includes Inspire, and that stage-three patient is where the discussion widens beyond the palate.
Body mass index gives patients numbers they can hold onto. In the He meta-analysis, long-term response was about sixty-four percent with a body mass index under thirty. It was about forty-two percent at thirty or above. The caveat: that was classic single-level UPPP, and fewer than a quarter of patients had individual data. In this paper, each point of body mass index meant roughly a third lower odds of success, but only within a lean cohort. Dr. Nord treats weight loss, including glucagon-like peptide one drugs, as part of multimodal treatment alongside Inspire, often both rather than either one alone.
Residual symptoms matter too. Satisfaction followed them closely, so in clinic, ask about snoring, unrefreshing sleep and fatigue, not just the AHI. And quote durability honestly, because early numbers like two in three tend to fall over the long term.
Confidence is high in the direction: anatomy and body mass index matter. Confidence is low in the model itself, because its area under the curve has never been tested outside the patients who built it. What would move it is external validation, ideally in a BRP cohort with DISE, longer follow-up and a validated satisfaction tool. Until then, the model is one to watch.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Ling X, Zheng J, Liu Q, Shi C, Fan C. Predictive factors for surgical outcomes and symptom persistence after uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. *Head Face Med*. 2026;22(1). doi:10.1186/s13005-026-00621-1 https://doi.org/10.1186/s13005-026-00621-1

item.description:
Here is the take-home point. Dr. Nord performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty and teaches residents in the operating room and clinic. The decision this paper touches is which palate operation to choose when DISE shows lateral wall or concentric collapse at the velum, and how to counsel that patient beforehand.
Hold on to the headline: E-S-P took the A-H-I from about twenty-one to about thirteen, and the muscle-sparing UPPP's fall was not statistically significant. What this adds is independent support for the principle behind B-R-P: palate surgery should reposition muscle and address the lateral wall, not just remove tissue. But this paper did not study B-R-P, and it should not be quoted as B-R-P evidence. Nothing in it argues for moving from B-R-P to E-S-P. The Neruntarat meta-analysis points to similar A-H-I results with a shorter operation for B-R-P.
For counseling, the paper adds frank morbidity numbers. After E-S-P, nearly a third of patients had a minor secondary bleed, and the top step of pain medicine was needed more often. The Innsbruck patients stayed five days. In Dr. Nord's practice, airway-surgery patients like these are kept for twenty-three-hour observation, so the Innsbruck pain and bleeding figures come from a much longer stay. Patients should also hear that palate surgery usually lowers the A-H-I rather than normalizing it. In this series, the average after E-S-P was still about thirteen events an hour, and twelve weeks says nothing about durability.
Weight belongs in that conversation. In this paper, a body mass index over twenty-five was linked to a worse postoperative A-H-I, though the size of that effect was not reported. An easy figure to quote comes from the Kaki study. Those patients averaged a body mass index of about thirty-two. Fewer than half met surgical success after E-S-P, twenty-four of fifty-two. The caveat is that this is a different cohort, scored with its own version of the success criteria, and it compares cohorts rather than measuring the effect of weight directly. Dr. Nord treats weight loss, including glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1, drugs, as part of multimodal treatment of O-S-A, often alongside Inspire rather than instead of it.
My confidence that lateral-wall operations beat tissue trimming is moderate. My confidence in the size of the E-S-P advantage here is low. What would move both is a randomized or matched comparison of B-R-P against E-S-P, with the same sleep test before and after, outcomes by DISE pattern, and follow-up past a year.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Steinbichler TB, Bender B, Hartl R, Strasser V, Sontheimer D, Buricic S, et al. Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty Versus Expansion Sphincter Pharyngoplasty: A Single Centre Experience. *Clocks & Sleep*. 2025;7(3):38. doi:10.3390/clockssleep7030038 https://doi.org/10.3390/clockssleep7030038

item.description:
The take-home point: this paper changes the counseling conversation and the follow-up questions. It doesn't change who is offered Inspire or how the implant is placed.
Dr. Nord is a high-volume Inspire implanter, so in Dr. Nord's practice the first decision this touches is consent. Tell candidates what this series showed: about one in six patients noticed a new sound when the device switched on, most often described as buzzing. For most, it was mild. Of the twelve who heard it, five said it had no effect on daily life, sleep or mood. None described a severe effect, and none stopped using the device. Then give the caveats plainly: one center, a telephone survey, an unvalidated questionnaire, no hearing tests, and an unknown response rate.
Preexisting tinnitus isn't a reason to exclude a patient. It isn't grounds for blanket reassurance either, because four against eight can't settle the question. Record tinnitus and hearing history before surgery, since this study had to rely on recall to decide that a sound was new.
The second decision comes at activation and titration. Ask directly: do you hear anything when the device turns on? Ask whether it's louder lying on the implant side. When a patient's use is slipping, ask whether noise is part of the reason. That link isn't proven here. But the registry data show that discomfort can cost hours of use, and without targeted questions this effect is easy to miss. If a sound is bothersome, reprogramming is a reasonable next step, though no one has shown it changes the sound.
The paper describes an approach that intentionally includes the C1 fibers to the geniohyoid. This study is no reason to drop them; the bone-conduction mechanism is a hypothesis.
The paper doesn't say which Inspire generation was implanted, and there are no published outcomes yet for Inspire V, so don't tie this figure to any one generation.
Confidence is moderate that these questions belong in follow-up, and low for the exact rate. What would move it is a multicenter prospective study that reports its response rate and includes audiometry, acoustic recordings, laterality, programming changes and longitudinal follow-up. If device sound turned out to drive nonuse or explantation, it would become a selection question, not just a counseling one.
The citation: Belilos, Adibi, Tucker, Saeedi, Calder, Lee, and Nord. Auditory Perceptions Associated With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea. Laryngoscope Investigative Otolaryngology, twenty twenty-six, volume eleven, article e seven zero five five zero.
Residents, what one question about sound will you add to your next activation visit?

Here is the take-home point. The decision this paper touches is what to offer a patient with moderate to severe sleep apnea who is not a good Inspire candidate. Often that is because of large tonsils, a high body mass index, or both. Dr. Nord's practice implants Inspire at high volume and performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, so this is a familiar fork in the road.
First, the paper sharpens counseling. In this series, the AHI was cut roughly in half, from about fifty to about twenty-three. Only about one in three was cured. Counsel with that residual AHI, not the nine-in-ten success figure, and plan with the patient for possible residual disease.
Second, it adds weight to treating large tonsils first, in line with Green and TEAMUP. Consider a patient with grade three or four tonsils who sits outside the Inspire window. For that patient, a tonsillectomy-based palate operation is a reasonable first step. This is one surgeon's uncontrolled series, so treat it as support, not proof.
Third, keep the Müller lateral wall finding as a hypothesis, not a selection rule.
Fourth, weight. Two figures are easy to share with patients. In the Green study, each one-point rise in body mass index meant about eight percent lower odds of responding to pharyngeal surgery. That is observational data across mixed palate techniques. For Inspire, the 2020 ADHERE registry analysis from Thaler in the Laryngoscope found that each one-point rise in body mass index meant about nine percent lower odds of success. It still calls a body mass index of thirty-two "a useful guide" for implant decisions. That is registry data, not a trial. In Dr. Nord's practice, weight loss, including glucagon-like peptide one drugs, is part of multimodal treatment of obstructive sleep apnea. It often runs alongside Inspire rather than instead of it. Many Inspire patients are already on these drugs or will become candidates for them. The South Carolina authors likewise suggest weight reduction alongside palate surgery when appropriate.
My confidence that the AHI roughly halves in patients like these is moderate. It is one surgeon, retrospective, uncontrolled, and six months long. What would raise it? A controlled comparison against tonsillectomy alone or against barbed reposition, and two-year results. For residents, the line to practice in clinic is simple: half the AHI, one in three cured.
Today's paper was Abdelwahab and colleagues, with Nguyen as senior author: "Preservation Palatopharyngoplasty for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Predictors and Clinical Outcomes." It appeared in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, 2026, volume one seventy-four, issue four, pages eleven-oh-two to eleven-oh-eight.

Often that is because of large tonsils, a high body mass index, or both. Dr. Nord's practice implants Inspire at high volume and performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, so this is a familiar fork in the road.

Second, it adds weight to treating large tonsils first, in line with Green and TEAMUP. Consider a patient with grade three or four tonsils who sits outside the Inspire window. For that patient, a tonsillectomy-based palate operation is a reasonable first step. This is one surgeon's uncontrolled series, so treat it as support, not proof.

Third, keep the Müller lateral wall finding as a hypothesis, not a selection rule.

Fourth, weight. Two figures are easy to share with patients. In the Green study, each one-point rise in body mass index meant about eight percent lower odds of responding to pharyngeal surgery. My confidence that the AHI roughly halves in patients like these is moderate. It is one surgeon, retrospective, uncontrolled, and six months long. What would raise it? item.title: Post-Operative Radiological Evaluation of a Bilateral Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation System
item.itunes:title: Post-Operative Radiological Evaluation of a Bilateral Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation System
item.description:
The take-home point is simple. For a patient with a Genio implant, the plain film is the image that shows the hardware. Every x-ray was clean, all eleven. Every CT carried artifact, all eight.
Dr. Nord's practice is built on high-volume Inspire implantation and barbed reposition pharyngoplasty. This is Genio data from eleven patients, so its numbers stay with Genio. What it adds is to counseling and to imaging.
When a patient asks about the bilateral device, the meta-analyses are the place to start. There's no demonstrated efficacy advantage over unilateral stimulation, and the safety record is less mature. DREAM adds device-specific failure modes, including migration. When a patient with a Genio implant needs imaging of the floor of mouth or tongue base, we now know what to expect. Plain films show the hardware cleanly. CT will carry artifact, compounded by dental work, and the authors advise reformatting in at least two planes. This is an older population where head and neck cancer workup will come up, as the authors point out, so tell the radiologist up front.
What I teach residents in the operating room and clinic is this. A symmetric film is not a prediction of success, and an asymmetric one is not grounds for revision. The trigger for workup is failure to activate or failure to respond, not the picture.
Confidence is moderate on the imaging advice, because it rests on eight CT scans in patients who all had dental implants. It's low on anything linking position to function. What would move it is a repeat film over time. That would tell us when migration happens, in the first week or the first month. It would show how often only one side shifts, and whether day-one asymmetry gets worse. Tie those films to thresholds and twelve-month A-H-I, and the day-one baseline becomes actionable. That's what to watch.
The citation: Kilgue, Gehl, Abolmaali, Scholtz, Scherl and Todt. Post-operative radiological evaluation of a bilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation system. Frontiers in Surgery, 2026, volume thirteen, article one eight one eight two four seven.

item.title: Exploring the Role of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Optimizing Upper Airway Stimulation Therapy for Non-Responders
item.itunes:title: Exploring the Role of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Optimizing Upper Airway Stimulation Therapy for Non-Responders
item.description:
The take-home point: Dr. Nord considers DISE with the stimulator on a good tool for the Inspire non-responder who tolerates the device, once awake endoscopy and reprogramming have failed. Copper's group gives a clear way to run it: settings first, then add-on therapy targeted to whatever stays obstructed.
The honest limit stays. The headline, about eighteen events an hour lower in the eighteen patients followed, is a real fall. But this uncontrolled series can't show that the DISE itself caused it, rather than the treatments that followed, time, or regression to the mean.
The paper doesn't alter who is offered an implant, since nothing at baseline predicted who would fail to couple. What it adds is to counselling the stuck patient. At this one hospital, about one implant in four needed this step, twenty-nine of one hundred and fourteen. A little over a quarter of those became responders, eight of twenty-nine. Quote that alongside eight of the eighteen followed, and don't call the higher figure a rescue rate.
Settings changes are the most hopeful branch, five of six. Dr. Nord performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, and after an implant, the honest expectation is that fewer than half respond: three of seven did. In Dr. Nord's practice, airway-surgery patients like these are kept for twenty-three-hour observation. None of the five who had an oral appliance or uvulectomy responded, though that group is tiny.
And Inspire V? The stimulation lead remains, so the configuration logic may carry over. That is untested; there are no published outcomes yet for Inspire V.
Dr. Nord's confidence in the size of the benefit is low to moderate. What would raise it is a comparison of DISE-guided management against repeated awake titration in matched non-responders, with every patient accounted for, follow-up to twelve months, and usage hours reported.
The paper is from Copper's group, in Sleep and Breathing, 2025, volume twenty-nine, article two eighty-five.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?

item.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
item.itunes:title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
item.description:
The take-home point: this paper sharpens how Dr. Nord's practice counsels patients about weight and surgery, even though it doesn't change who is offered surgery.
The decision it touches is the conversation with a patient who carries excess weight and is considering Inspire or barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, BRP. In Dr. Nord's practice, weight loss, including GLP-1 drugs, is part of multimodal treatment of obstructive sleep apnea alongside Inspire, often both rather than either-or. Many Inspire patients are already on these drugs or will become candidates for them.
So quote the drug-specific headline, not the pooled ten: about twenty-two fewer events per hour than control with tirzepatide over a year, about six fewer with liraglutide.
Two more figures patients can hold onto. In the meta-regression from Bednarik's group, about a ten percent drop in body mass index matched about a thirty-six percent drop in the A-H-I. A twenty percent drop matched about fifty-seven percent. A thirty percent drop matched about sixty-nine. The gains shrink beyond twenty percent, these are averages across study arms rather than predictions for one patient, and Lilly funded the work.
In the ADHERE registry, from Mehra's group, in the European Respiratory Journal in 2019, with prior-generation Inspire II and Inspire IV devices, each one-point rise in body mass index meant about nine percent lower odds of success. Put the other way, a lower body mass index went with better odds, a fair reason to encourage weight loss, though the registry measured baseline weight, not weight lost.
On oxygen, be precise: the pooled desaturation index and lowest saturation were not statistically significant, while the tirzepatide trials did show a lower hypoxic burden. Don't promise a cardiovascular benefit, and don't call these drugs a substitute for CPAP; the authors don't either. If a patient loses substantial weight before surgery, get a new sleep study before deciding.
What would sharpen this? A randomized trial of a GLP-1 drug before Inspire or BRP, measuring candidacy and surgical response. Data beyond fifty-two weeks, including what happens after stopping. And repeat drug-induced sleep endoscopy after weight loss, to see whether the collapse pattern changes.
Again, that's Aljazeeri's group, "GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials." Sleep and Breathing, 2026, volume thirty, article two seventy-nine.
Residents, what's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Carvalhal G, Mora MMR, Peralta-Jiménez GA, Ayasa L, Barrera V, Advani K, et al. GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. *Sleep Breath*. 2026. doi:10.1007/s11325-026-03826-5 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11325-026-03826-5

item.itunes:title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
item.description:
The take-home point: pain about three out of ten on day one and near zero by one month is a promising early-recovery signal. But it describes one technique, in thirty selected patients, under one fixed protocol.
The first decision it touches is technique choice. In Dr. Nord's practice, B-R-P remains the palate operation of choice. This paper offers an appealing muscle-sparing idea, but no head-to-head data. The evidence that would move that decision is a direct comparison with B-R-P under identical steroids and analgesia. It would need blinded pain scoring, visits through the first two weeks, and sleep testing well beyond six months.
The second decision is counseling. The paper adds a carefully measured early recovery curve. Those numbers belong to the stayed bridge technique, so they should be quoted only as stayed bridge data. For a patient having B-R-P, the counseling numbers still come from the B-R-P series. About one in five have transient swallowing difficulty that settles within a week. Thread extrusion happens in about one in eight across barbed techniques. This paper adds one useful line: sparing the muscle did not make extrusion go away.
The third decision is observation. These patients stayed two days by protocol. In Dr. Nord's practice, airway-surgery patients like these are kept for twenty-three-hour observation. The twelve-hour scores fall inside that window. The twenty-four- and forty-eight-hour scores come after it. The paper did not monitor breathing on the first night, so it can't inform how long that observation should be.
Finally, the Inspire conversation. Dr. Nord is a high-volume Inspire implanter. Patients with this profile, moderate disease, a body mass index under thirty and tonsils present, are the group where Inspire and palate surgery are both on the table. This paper is palate-surgery data. It gives no outcomes by collapse pattern and no post-operative DISE. It adds recovery information on the palate side of that discussion, not Inspire evidence.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Pace A, Iannella G, Maniaci A, Cocuzza S, Moffa A, Alunni Fegatelli D, et al. Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP). *JCM*. 2025;14(20):7402. doi:10.3390/jcm14207402 https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm14207402

item.title: Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes
item.itunes:title: Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes
item.description:
The call for Dr. Nord's practice is no change, with a watch on ultrasound as a research tool.
The decision this paper touches is what to make of tongue motion after implantation. Three pieces.
First, counseling. I won't tell a patient that a strong forward tongue at activation predicts a great sleep study, or that a modest one predicts failure. This paper gives no basis for either, and the Emory data say the same.
Second, titration. There's no support here for using visible or ultrasound motion as a titration target, or for raising amplitude just to make the tongue move more. Motion wasn't related to voltage in their standard-configuration patients. The authors caution against increasing stimulation beyond comfort. That's sensible, but it's their recommendation, not something this study measured.
Third, the non-responder whose tongue moves well. This paper and the Penn work both point away from making the tongue move more, and toward the airway itself. In Dr. Nord's practice, once awake endoscopy and reprogramming have failed, DISE is a good tool for the Inspire non-responder, because it shows the lumen that ultrasound can't. The authors suggest residual palatal or lateral-wall obstruction as one explanation, a hypothesis they didn't test. That's where palate surgery, including barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, enters the discussion, but this paper isn't evidence for it.
What doesn't change? This study says nothing about retraction, or about which nerve branches the cuff captures at implantation. That question still rests on Steffen's group's small series. When I teach residents in the operating room, the point is narrower now: how far the tongue moves forward is not a demonstrated predictor of the sleep study.
Confidence: moderate that graded ultrasound magnitude and symmetry aren't useful predictors at this level of measurement. Low on buckling, where the interval is wide. What would move me is a prospective study with measured displacement, several amplitudes per patient, paired DISE, one standardized full-night study, and adjustment for baseline severity.
The citation: Tschopp, Janjic, Caversaccio, Borner and Tschopp. "Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes." Laryngoscope Investigative Otolaryngology, twenty twenty-six. Volume eleven, issue two.
Residents, what's your one takeaway?

item.itunes:title: Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Experts on Tongue, Hypopharynx, and Supraglottis Associated With Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Part 1 - Evaluation and Decision Making
item.description:
What is the bottom line for my clinical practice? My explicit call on this paper is watch, accompanied by immediate operational reinforcement of our existing surgical protocols.
This paper does not require an immediate change in operative technique because it represents expert consensus on diagnostic workup and decision-making rather than a comparative trial. However, it provides robust peer-reviewed support for four clinical decisions in our practice.
First, regarding Inspire hypoglossal nerve stimulation candidacy: this consensus strongly supports our staging algorithm. When an adult presents with severe tongue base collapse on sleep endoscopy but also carries grade three or four palatine tonsils, statement twenty-one provides unanimous consensus backing to perform tonsillectomy and palate expansion first. We do not implant a neurostimulator through obstructing palatine tonsils. During pre-implant sleep endoscopy, we must also evaluate the supraglottic phenotypes detailed here. If you identify primary trapdoor or floppy epiglottic collapse folding over the laryngeal inlet, unilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation alone may fail to recruit the epiglottis if the lingual surface is not directly tethered to the advancing tongue base.
